extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament, policymakers, journalists, and the informed public interested in the Hutton inquiry and government/media accountability
extracted.subtask_description: Hansard transcript of a House of Lords debate taking note of Lord Hutton's report into the circumstances surrounding Dr David Kelly's death, including discussion of the report's findings, media conduct, government procedures and the scope of a subsequent inquiry. The page records evaluative principles and procedural expectations voiced by peers about inquiries, intelligence use, and press behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry independence and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry should be independent, transparent in process and produce clear analysis of evidence; judges are appointed to analyse the evidence and reach findings of fact rather than seek compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praising Lord Hutton: 'His conduct of the inquiry has been regarded as exemplary because of the transparency of the process, and the clarity with which the evidence unfolded.' 'Judges are not selected to produce a compromise; they are asked to analyse the evidence and reach findings of fact.' Expect dispassionate, non‑political analysis; judge competence and procedural openness are emphasised as key virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish false allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Media outlets should not publish false allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rule cited from the report: 'do not publish false allegations.' Used as a baseline legal/journalistic standard and linked to established case law (Reynolds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial awareness before broadcasting serious attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should know the terms in which a serious attack on the Government (or other subject) is going to be made before it is broadcast and consider whether it is right in all the circumstances to broadcast it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted standard: 'it is necessary to ensure that the editors of media outlets know the terms in which a serious attack is going to be made on the Government before it is broadcast and consider whether it is right in all the circumstances to broadcast it.' Serves as guidance for editorial processes and pre‑broadcast checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate alleged inaccuracies before dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an allegation of inaccuracy is made, the management should normally investigate it before dismissing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a management responsibility: reporters' or programmes' alleged inaccuracies should prompt internal investigation rather than immediate dismissal; applied in discussion of BBC/Gilligan.

rubrics_metrics.name: When PM and JIC allege falsity governors should investigate
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Prime Minister and the chairman of the Joint Intelligence Committee allege to the governors of a public broadcaster that a broadcast is false, the governors should investigate the allegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular procedural expectation placed on institutional governors (e.g., BBC governors) to examine official allegations of false reporting rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'sexed‑up' — no embellishment with known false intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The dossier must not be 'sexed-up' in the sense of being embellished with items of intelligence known or believed to be false or unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quotation/paraphrase from Hutton: 'The term 'sexed-up' ... could mean that the dossier was embellished with items of intelligence known or believed to be false or unreliable.' That meaning was treated as unacceptable and 'unfounded' in the context of the Gilligan broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'sexed‑up' — drafting to maximise strength within available intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatively, 'sexed-up' can mean drafting the dossier to make the case against the subject as strong as the intelligence contained in it permitted (i.e., emphasising an argument to its strongest reasonable form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hutton's second possible meaning: 'whilst the intelligence contained in the dossier was believed to be reliable, the dossier was drafted in such a way as to make the case against Saddam Hussein as strong as the intelligence contained in it permitted.' This raises a separate evaluative standard about appropriate drafting and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper caveating and faithful wording of intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence assessments used in public dossiers should be caveated appropriately and wording should not be strengthened (e.g., changing 'may' to 'are') without clear basis in the intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples criticised: change from 'Iraq may be able to deploy chemical or biological weapons within 45 minutes' to 'The Iraq military are able to deploy these weapons within 45 minutes.' Guidance: avoid altering modality or certainty in ways that materially change the claim unless evidence supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIC independence and limitation of political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Joint Intelligence Committee (and intelligence authors) should provide independent assessments; political or press officers should not unduly influence the substantive content of intelligence products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: influential press/political operatives (e.g., Alastair Campbell) seeking to 'improve' wording or to chair JIC meetings; risk of 'subconscious' influence leading to stronger wording than warranted. Expectation: preserve institutional boundaries and expert input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation of technical experts before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant subject‑matter experts (e.g., CW/BW specialists) should be consulted and their detailed input read and considered before publication of intelligence assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited failure: experienced DIS experts (Dr Brian Jones) felt their detailed caveats were not properly read; guidance implies editorial processes should ensure expert caveats are heeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of sources and disclosure to parliamentary committees
rubrics_metrics.description: If government knows the likely source of a journalist's allegation relevant to parliamentary inquiries, there is a duty to consider disclosure to the parliamentary committees undertaking inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: who was the source of Gilligan's broadcast? Government officers debated whether to disclose to FAC/ISC. Guidance: withholding material relevant to parliamentary scrutiny is problematic; how and when to disclose must be carefully managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for notifying named civil servants
rubrics_metrics.description: If a civil servant's name is to be confirmed to the press, the employing department should explicitly inform that person beforehand and must have a procedure to inform them immediately if their name has been confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hutton found MoD at fault for not informing Dr Kelly that its press office would confirm his name and for allowing 1.5 hours to elapse before telling him. Recommended measures: amendments to terms of employment, disciplinary procedures, and rapid notification processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and guidance for civil servants under media pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should provide assistance and guidance to civil servants at risk of media attention, including clear rules that no-one should speak to media without express approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MoD committed to examine assistance and guidance; principle remains 'no-one should speak to the media, on or off the record, without express approval.' Support mechanisms and disciplinary clarity recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of press releases and agreed timing when naming individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person's identity is to be disclosed to the press, it is preferable to issue a press statement at an agreed time after close discussion with the individual to minimise harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hutton recommended a press release and close discussion with Dr Kelly would have been better; guidance discourages ad hoc confirmation that surprises the individual and allows no preparation or support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and apply findings of inquiries rather than cherry‑picking
rubrics_metrics.description: Public and political actors should accept the findings of a properly conducted independent inquiry and draw policy and procedural conclusions from them, rather than selectively using parts of the report to score political points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated exhortations in debate: 'We will make so much more progress if we accept those findings and then draw our conclusions from them.' Anti‑pattern: 'cherry‑pick bits of it to make political points.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial control and management responsibility in broadcasting organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasting organisations must have effective editorial control and management oversight over journalists and programmes to prevent serious errors and hold staff to account when mistakes occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: BBC management and editorial control over Andrew Gilligan were judged weak; this led to departures/resignations. Recommendation: strengthen editorial oversight and internal checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of reference clarity for follow‑on inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms of reference for subsequent inquiries must be clear about scope (e.g., whether 'use of intelligence by Government' includes ministers and officials) so the committee can start with a common understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate on Butler inquiry terms: repeated calls for clarity; guidance that the committee chair should interpret scope but explicit drafting avoids early disputes. Example: government clarified that 'use of intelligence by government' includes ministers and officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure practice for Law Officers' advice
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Attorney‑General's full legal advice is normally not disclosed, providing a summary of the legal basis for actions (e.g., use of force) aids public evaluation and debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Chancellor explained modern practice: Law Officers' advice not normally disclosed; nevertheless a summary of legal basis was provided in the war context. Trade‑off between confidentiality norms and public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of eminent chairmen for complex intelligence inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex inquiries into national intelligence matters should be chaired by persons of recognised eminence and impartiality to ensure confidence in the process and findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate welcomed figures like Lord Butler and Lord Inge to chair Butler inquiry; expectation that eminent chairs will ensure the inquiry is given time and space and judged on the quality of findings rather than preconceived views.
